about: Every example in the kit, as the menu shows it (T24). One file, read by the menu and by scripts/check_demos.py, which holds each card to its make target, its page and the scene it opens: a technique is named here once, with the classes that are evidence of it, and a card naming a technique its scene never reaches by use -- constructed, called or extended, not merely typed or read a constant of -- fails the gate. A card whose example offers a choice of controllers lists them, and names the roster table they are cycled from; the gate holds the two to each other (T63). A card says what the AI decides, which techniques decide it and what part each plays, and what to watch on screen.

perception.name: a vision cone, line of sight and hearing

htn.name: an HTN, a hierarchical task network

pure-pursuit.name: pure pursuit: steer at a point down the line

speed-profile.name: a speed profile, braked for backwards from the corners

pid-control.name: a PID controller: push from the error now, summed, and changing

heat-line.name: Melder's heat line: where across the road to be among other cars

measured-grip.name: a car measured before the race: the grip and braking it really has

strips.name: STRIPS planning, over a domain written in PDDL

case-lookup.name: a lookup of recorded situations (a ghost)

priority-queue.name: a priority queue of wishes, the shipped RTS economy

team-commander.name: a commander over an influence map

squad-confidence.name: squad confidence, and retreat in waves

stealth-senses.name: a vision shape read as certainty, light at the feet, and hearing along the level

awareness.name: awareness that rises, falls a phase at a time, and holds after an alert

belief-map.name: a belief over where the player may be, spread and cleared by sight

search-coordinator.name: a search shared out by claims

role-arbiter.name: fight roles granted by an arbiter

weighed-actions.name: every action scored by its considerations, the highest done

monte-carlo-tree-search.name: Monte Carlo tree search: random playouts, spent by UCB1 on the moves that do well

target-tile.name: a target tile, and the shortest straight line to it: the arcade's ghosts

value-iteration.name: value iteration: an MDP solved in Python, its policy looked up

director.name: a director: the player's intensity paces the threats, after Left 4 Dead

constraints.name: constraint satisfaction: AC-3 and backtracking place the level

discourse-acts.name: a language model reads the player's words as one declared act, behind a validator

examples.title: Checkers
examples.decides: Which move white plays: it looks a few moves ahead for both sides and picks the line that leaves it best off.

techniques.part: searches every line of play to a fixed depth, assuming you answer as well as you can, and skips lines that cannot matter
E swaps the hand-written way of scoring a position for weights Python fitted to self-play

examples.controls: click a piece, then a lit square; space plays white's move; 1-6 sets how far it looks; E swaps its evaluation
examples.watch: Every move white considered, with the value it worked out; the pink arrow is the one it will play, and the panel spells out the line it expects.

examples.title: Noughts and crosses
examples.decides: Which square crosses takes: it draws a bead from the matchbox for this position, and squares with more beads are likelier.

techniques.part: the beads in each box were added and taken away by thousands of games played beforehand, in Python
M shows what a perfect player makes of each square, to compare with what the machine learnt

examples.controls: space draws MENACE's bead; click a square; 1-4 sets its age; M shows perfect play
examples.watch: The beads on each empty square, as a number, a bar and a chance, before the bead is drawn.

examples.title: Four searches
examples.decides: Which route to take from the start to the goal, and which cells are worth looking at on the way.

techniques.part: spreads in rings: the fewest steps, blind to what a cell costs
bolts down one corridor and takes the first route it stumbles on
spreads in rings weighted by cost: the cheapest route
the cheapest route too, but leans towards the goal and stops early

examples.controls: 1-4 choose the search; space reveals one more cell, enter the rest; drag to paint walls and mud; B steps through boards
examples.watch: The frontier spreading cell by cell, in the order the search looked at them.

examples.title: The skirmish
examples.decides: Whether each blue unit takes the fight in reach or backs off, and which node it walks to.

techniques.part: a combat model gives the chance of winning a fight, and a capture model which node blue can hold soonest
the route a unit walks once it knows where it is going

examples.controls: click a unit, then a neighbouring cell; space ends the turn; R starts again
examples.watch: Every blue unit's reason in the status beside the board, with the probability the model computed.

examples.title: Stealth
examples.decides: How suspicious each guard is, and so whether it keeps to its round, goes to look, or gives chase.

techniques.part: what each guard can see and hear: its cone, the walls and trees in the way, the light, your footsteps
turns what it saw and heard into a suspicion that rises and falls, rather than a yes or a no
D shows the danger map: how watched each cell is
the route a guard walks to where it thinks you are

examples.controls: arrows walk; shift sprints; space waits; D shows the danger map; R starts again
examples.watch: Each guard's suspicion bar and its state colour, and the terms of its controller written out under the room.

examples.title: One guard, four ways to decide
examples.decides: What the guard does next -- patrol, look, chase or catch -- written four ways you can swap while it walks.

techniques.part: snaps from state to state when a condition says so
asks the whole tree again every turn, so it reconsiders
plans backwards from a goal to the cheapest chain of actions, every turn
breaks a task into steps and carries on down the method it chose

examples.controls: space plays a turn, enter ten; 1-4 swap the brain; R starts again
examples.watch: The brain's panel: the state, the tree's path or the plan, with the step being run lit.

examples.title: Steering: seek, arrive, pursue, avoid
examples.decides: How hard each vehicle turns and brakes, right now -- not which cell to go to, but which way to push and how much.

techniques.part: full speed at the cross, so it overshoots and swings back through it forever
seek that brakes inside a circle round the cross, so it stops on it
seek aimed at where the running dot will be, never more than a second ahead
swerves from the first obstacle on the stretch ahead, added to seek with twice its weight

examples.controls: click in an arena to move its cross; space pauses, . steps one sixtieth of a second, R starts again
examples.watch: The orange arrow -- the force the behaviour asks for -- against the blue one, where the vehicle is going: seek's never shrinks at the cross, arrive's turns to brake as it enters its circle.

examples.title: Racing: you against an AI in the same car
examples.decides: Where the AI steers and how fast it dares to go, every frame -- in the same car as yours, so if it is faster it drives better, never a better car.

techniques.part: the white dot: a point a lookahead distance down the racing line, which the AI steers at; harder AIs look further, so they turn in earlier
says which way to go for the dot; pure pursuit's formula turns that angle into how hard to turn
the line's colour: the fastest each point allows at the grip this AI dares, carried back from every corner at its braking; the white bar is where it must already be braking

examples.controls: arrows or WASD drive; 1-3 choose the AI and start again; R again, P pause, . one step while paused; Tab watches the three AIs race (1-3 follow one, A alone)
examples.watch: Race the easy AI, then the hard one, and follow it into a corner: its white bar shows where it starts braking, and the hard one brakes later. Down a straight you are as fast as it is -- same car, same top speed.

examples.title: Racing in 3D: tyres that slip, and drivers that measure their car (3D)
examples.decides: How fast the road ahead allows, where to steer, and where across the road to be among other cars -- on a car whose tyres slip, so the driver measures it first and corrects as it goes.

techniques.part: before the start, on the test pad: each car cornered to the limit and braked hard; the driver races on what its own car did, not on its sheet (3 switches to the sheet)
the white bar on the road: where the car must already be braking, from the bends it sees ahead and the grip it measured; the hard car's bar comes later
the white post: the point a lookahead of seconds down the line, which the car steers at
the trace under the panel: how far the watched car is from where it wants to be; 1 drops the integral and derivative, and the car swings off
the coloured posts across the road ahead of the watched car, and the yellow ball rolling to the coolest place; 2 switches to reacting to one rival at a time

examples.controls: arrows or WASD drive; 1 PID full or proportional only, 2 heat line or one rival at a time, 3 grip measured or off the sheet; Tab watches the next car, C the camera, T the other track, R again, Space pause
examples.watch: Watch the measuring first: the sheet promises more grip and braking than the car has. Then follow the hard car into a corner and watch its tyres go yellow, not red. Press 3 and it brakes for a car it is not driving, and slides off. Press T: the drivers find their line on a track nobody tuned them on.

examples.title: Real-time strategy against a commander that plans
examples.decides: What to build next and when, and where each squad of fighters goes -- against a clock that does not wait while it thinks.

techniques.part: the commander plans the build order to its goal -- workers, magma, room, barracks, lab, mortars -- and each step's wait is worked out by jumping to the moment it is affordable
H swaps the commander's planner for an HTN, whose orders are the designer's, over the same domain
the economy under the plan: the top wish waits for its price and nothing below it is bought meanwhile; V hands your side to the queues alone
each squad scores every region by worth, odds and distance, and goes to the best
the computer's belief about who holds the map, the enemy half remembered through the fog and fading; I draws it
each squad gathers, advances, fights or falls back, and the arrow it took is written beside it
a squad's members follow one field to their region, shared by everyone going there

examples.controls: drag to select, right click to move, attack or gather; B D L T E build with a worker, W 1 2 3 train; space pauses, + and - change the speed, V watches two computers, C the level, H the planner, I the influence map, F lifts the fog from the screen, R again
examples.watch: The panel's plan: each step's wait counts down, and when the commander sees what you build, its goal changes to the counter and the plan is redrawn. On the board, a squad's dashed line is where it chose to go and the numbers are every region's score -- press I and see how much it believes is where it last saw it.

examples.title: Tactics against the computer
examples.decides: Two modes of one game, chosen here with M or in the game with M. Advance Wars: for every computer piece, where it walks, what it attacks, and what its workshop builds -- by whichever controller C picks. XCOM: for the computer's piece about to act, where it walks and whom it shoots, on what its side sees through the fog.

techniques.part: the default: a written priority list, the baseline everything else is measured against
the planner: a plan of steps searched with A* over facts about the board, replanned every few turns
the learned controller asks a trained model whether to take each fight
the easy, normal and hard levels weigh each move one or two plies ahead with the fight's exact odds
one of four teams written from the guard's four ways to decide
another of the four
another, its actions priced in turns
the fourth
the threat map tinted on the board: how many enemy pieces could strike each cell
XCOM's first enemy: every walk and shot of the piece about to act scored on its side's view -- the shot it leaves, the fire it walks into, cover and flanks in both -- the best taken

XCOM's second enemy: the piece's options and the turns after them searched by random playouts, on the board its side believes in -- each option's visits drawn growing a frame at a time, space stopping it early

examples.controls: click a unit, then a lit cell; click an enemy to attack or shoot; W waits; 1-5 build; Z undoes; space ends the turn; C changes the computer; S swaps sides; M the other mode; T the threat map (in XCOM: each enemy's chance against the cell under the cursor); V, in XCOM, what the computer sees
examples.watch: Each computer decision drawn on the board before it is played, with the reason in the status. In XCOM, the board shows what the computer sees, and every option it weighed for the piece about to act: its score, and its best hit chance; your own shots show their chance on the target before you click. With MCTS (C), a bar of visits for each of the piece's options grows while it thinks, then the line of play it expects; space plays what it believes so far.

examples.title: Fighting, training mode
examples.decides: What the dummy does on each frame it is allowed to decide: guard, strike, throw, jump or evade.

techniques.part: the fixed opponent's hand-written answers to the situations it recognises, at three levels
it sees the fight a quarter of a second late, as a person would
the learner counts your habits during the fight and leans towards the answer to them
the bandit keeps, for each situation, what each of its answers earned against you, and tries the one UCB1 ranks first
the ghosts look up what a recorded player did in the same situation
the clone is a model fitted to that player's fights

examples.controls: A/D walk, W jumps, S crouches; U/I punch, J/K kick, L throws, O evades; M cycles the dummy; P pauses, space one frame
examples.watch: The panel: what the opponent saw, on which frame, and what it chose.

examples.title: Bot match: two teams of bots, capture and hold (3D)
examples.decides: Where each bot stands, which point each squad is sent to, and when a squad falls back -- on both teams, each switch yours to turn off.

techniques.part: the discs round the watched bot: every spot it weighed, coloured by why it was kept or dropped, its score above it; a teammate's claim closes a spot
the map's arrows: each squad sent to a point by worth and distance, over the team's influence (the map's colours)
the bar under each squad on the map, with its retreat and attack marks: below the first it falls back in two waves
each bot's walk to its spot, over a one-metre grid of the arena
the panel: every action, posture and pace the watched bot weighed, each with its score, the one taken marked, and each errand as its gain less its costs (V shows it while you play a bot)

examples.controls: 1/2/3 blue's claims, commander, retreat (Shift: red's); Tab watches the next bot, T takes it over (WASD, mouse, click, R reload, Ctrl crouch) and gives it back; M the other team's map, C camera, F fast, P pause, Space one decision, N new match
examples.watch: Turn blue's claims off and watch two blue bots end up behind the same box. Turn off the commander and watch the map's arrows: each blue bot is sent to its own nearest point not yet blue's, and the orders bunch onto fewer points. The score is the fight's, not the techniques': see docs/godot/botmatch.md.

examples.title: Infiltration: guards that notice, search together and call for help (3D)
examples.decides: How sure each guard is that it saw or heard you, where it believes you are, and whether to look, search, report, call for help or fight -- each guard weighing its own actions, the team sharing out the search.

techniques.part: the outlines round each guard: its vision zones, wide and sure near, narrow and doubtful far; the lines to your head, chest and feet, green where it sees them; the floor's brightness, the light it reads; the blue marks, how far a sound reached along the level
the bar over each guard: how aware it is, its phases' thresholds as ticks; it falls a phase at a time and stays cautious after an alert
how fast the bar fills: a fuzzy controller of how sure the eye is, the light, your motion and the distance (4 makes it a plain yes-or-no)

the orange cells: where the watched guard believes you are, spreading while it cannot see you and cleared where it looks (1 swaps it for a particle filter, its guesses drawn as dots; 1 again turns the belief off: guards walk to where they last saw you and give up)
the purple cross: the spot the watched guard was given to search; grey crosses, spots searched (2 turns claims off: they search the same places)
the role beside an alert guard's phase: one flanker at most, the rest shoot (3 turns it off: everyone who can shoot does)
the panel: every action the watched guard could take and its score, the one taken marked
each guard's walk to where it chose to go, over the level's walk grid and its stairs

the strip under the map (6 turns it on): your intensity over the last minute against the peak line, the phase -- building up, holding the peak, fading, relaxing -- and a mark for each reserve guard sent or called back, with a line on the map to where its patrol starts

on a generated level, K: the level declared and solved instead of drawn -- every route near a hiding place, a dark way to the exit, no post in sight of the start; K again replays the solver: the places left for what it places next, the ones propagation crossed out, what each refusal broke

examples.controls: WASD walk, mouse camera, C crouch, Z prone, Shift sprint, G throw a distraction, E take down from behind, click shoot; 1 belief (grid, particles, off), 2 coordinator, 3 arbiter, 4 accumulator, 5 off-screen halving, 6 director; K how a generated level is made (drawn, solved, solved and shown); Tab next guard, H hide the reasoning, L next level, N again, P pause, Space one decision
examples.watch: Crouch in the dark and watch a guard's bar fill slowly and fall back while you lie still. Get seen, then hide: the orange belief spreads from where it saw you, the others hear its radio report, and the purple crosses share the search out. Press 1 and hide again: the belief is a cloud of particles that walk on as a person would and thin where a guard looks. Press 1 once more: without a belief they walk to where they saw you and give up.

examples.title: Pac-Man: a small maze, and ghosts by the arcade's rules
examples.decides: Which way each ghost turns at the next fork: the way whose next cell is nearest its target tile -- your cell in chase, its home corner in scatter -- never back the way it came, except when the mode changes.

techniques.part: each ghost's target, every way it may take with the straight-line distance from the cell beyond, the way it chose; in chase a roll of the dice may overrule it, a rule of this game
with C, Pac-Man's move: the policy value iteration computed in Python for Blinky chasing for ever, looked up, with every cell's value and each move's worth drawn

examples.controls: arrows or WASD walk; V the ghosts' view; G brings Pinky in; C hands Pac-Man to the MDP; P pauses, space one step; R again
examples.watch: The crossed square is the ghost's target and the numbers on its ways are each next cell's distance to it: the white way is the smallest, chosen before the ghost moves. Orange with a die is the dice overruling it. Watch Blinky leave you for his corner when scatter begins, turning back at once. With C the MDP plays: green cells are worth much to Pac-Man, red ones a catch to come, and the boxed number beside him is the move it takes.

examples.title: Suck Up!'s doorstep: talk your way past the guard
examples.decides: Which act each of your lines was -- a role claimed, a paper shown, a name, a question, flattery, a threat, a bribe -- read by a local language model, which also voices the guard; then the scene's rules, not the model, move his trust and suspicion and open the door or sound the alarm.

techniques.part: the model reads your line as one of the scene's acts and voices Bram; the validator admits the act or refuses the reply, and a refused reply is the guard's own line, never an action

examples.controls: 1-9 say a recorded line; V the reasoning; R again; Tab types to a live local model (one already running, or one the game starts and stops), Enter says it
examples.watch: Three dots over Bram mean the model is answering while the game keeps drawing. With V, each line shows the act the model read and its argument, or why the validator refused it, then the rule that fired and how the green trust bar and the red suspicion bar moved against their white marks. Words that say the door opens open nothing: only the act counts.
